title: Monthly Sales Line Chart
markdown:
### The Scenario
A small online shop wants a simple visual of monthly sales to share in a team check-in.

### The Task
- Use `plt.plot()` to create a line chart of `months` vs `sales`.
- Set the chart title to `Monthly Sales Trend`.
- Set the x-axis label to `Month`.
- Set the y-axis label to `Sales ($)`.
- Display the chart.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

months = ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun']
sales = [1200, 1350, 1280, 1500, 1625, 1700]

# Create your chart below



plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) == 1, 'We expected exactly one line on the chart.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Monthly Sales Trend', 'Set the title to exactly "Monthly Sales Trend".'
assert ax.get_xlabel() == 'Month', 'Set the x-axis label to exactly "Month".'
assert ax.get_ylabel() == 'Sales ($)', 'Set the y-axis label to exactly "Sales ($)".'
hints: Start by plotting the month names on the x-axis and the sales values on the y-axis.
Use `plt.plot()` for the line, then add `plt.title()`, `plt.xlabel()`, and `plt.ylabel()`.
Try `plt.plot(months, sales)` followed by `plt.title('Monthly Sales Trend')`, `plt.xlabel('Month')`, and `plt.ylabel('Sales ($)')`.
solution_code:
plt.plot(months, sales)
plt.title('Monthly Sales Trend')
plt.xlabel('Month')
plt.ylabel('Sales ($)')

title: Daily Temperature with Markers
markdown:
### The Scenario
A local weather station wants a quick chart showing temperature changes across a week.

### The Task
- Use `plt.plot()` to graph `days` vs `temperature`.
- Add circle markers to each point.
- Set the title to `Weekly Temperature`.
- Set the y-axis label to `Temperature (C)`.
- Display the chart.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

days = ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun']
temperature = [29, 30, 31, 30, 32, 33, 31]

# Create your chart below



plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) == 1, 'We expected exactly one line on the chart.'
line = ax.lines[0]
assert line.get_marker() == 'o', 'Add circle markers using marker="o".'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Weekly Temperature', 'Set the title to exactly "Weekly Temperature".'
assert ax.get_ylabel() == 'Temperature (C)', 'Set the y-axis label to exactly "Temperature (C)".'
hints: This is a basic line chart, but each point should be highlighted with a marker.
Use `plt.plot()` and pass `marker='o'`.
Try `plt.plot(days, temperature, marker='o')`, then `plt.title('Weekly Temperature')` and `plt.ylabel('Temperature (C)')`.
solution_code:
plt.plot(days, temperature, marker='o')
plt.title('Weekly Temperature')
plt.ylabel('Temperature (C)')

title: Heart Rate Style Practice
markdown:
### The Scenario
A fitness coach is reviewing how a runner's heart rate changed during a workout.

### The Task
- Use `plt.plot()` to graph `minutes` vs `heart_rate`.
- Make the line green.
- Use a dashed line style.
- Set the title to `Heart Rate Over Time`.
- Display the chart.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

minutes = [0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25]
heart_rate = [78, 88, 96, 101, 99, 90]

# Create your chart below



plt.show()
validation_code:
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) == 1, 'We expected exactly one line on the chart.'
line = ax.lines[0]
assert mcolors.to_rgba(line.get_color()) == mcolors.to_rgba('green'), 'The line should be green.'
assert line.get_linestyle() == '--', 'The line should use a dashed linestyle.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Heart Rate Over Time', 'Set the title to exactly "Heart Rate Over Time".'
hints: You already know how to make a line chart; now focus on line styling.
Use `plt.plot()` with `color='green'` and `linestyle='--'`.
Try `plt.plot(minutes, heart_rate, color='green', linestyle='--')` and then `plt.title('Heart Rate Over Time')`.
solution_code:
plt.plot(minutes, heart_rate, color='green', linestyle='--')
plt.title('Heart Rate Over Time')

title: Compare Two Product Lines
markdown:
### The Scenario
A store manager wants to compare quarterly sales for two products on the same chart.

### The Task
- Plot `product_a` against `quarters`.
- Plot `product_b` against `quarters` on the same chart.
- Label the lines `Product A` and `Product B`.
- Show a legend.
- Set the title to `Quarterly Product Comparison`.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

quarters = ['Q1', 'Q2', 'Q3', 'Q4']
product_a = [120, 140, 160, 180]
product_b = [100, 135, 155, 190]

# Create your chart below



plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) == 2, 'We expected exactly two lines on the chart.'
legend = ax.get_legend()
assert legend is not None, 'Show a legend using plt.legend().'
labels = {text.get_text() for text in legend.get_texts()}
assert labels == {'Product A', 'Product B'}, 'The legend labels must be Product A and Product B.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Quarterly Product Comparison', 'Set the title to exactly "Quarterly Product Comparison".'
hints: You need two separate lines on the same axes so the trends can be compared directly.
Use `plt.plot()` twice, give each line a `label`, and then call `plt.legend()`.
Try `plt.plot(quarters, product_a, label='Product A')` and `plt.plot(quarters, product_b, label='Product B')`, then `plt.legend()` and `plt.title('Quarterly Product Comparison')`.
solution_code:
plt.plot(quarters, product_a, label='Product A')
plt.plot(quarters, product_b, label='Product B')
plt.legend()
plt.title('Quarterly Product Comparison')

title: Study Hours Scatter Plot
markdown:
### The Scenario
A teacher wants to see whether more study time is linked to higher quiz scores.

### The Task
- Use `plt.scatter()` to create a scatter plot of `study_hours` vs `quiz_score`.
- Set the title to `Study Hours vs Quiz Score`.
- Set the x-axis label to `Study Hours`.
- Set the y-axis label to `Quiz Score`.
- Display the chart.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

study_hours = [1, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6]
quiz_score = [55, 60, 64, 68, 74, 81, 88]

assert ax.get_xlabel() == 'Study Hours', 'Set the x-axis label to exactly "Study Hours".'

Use `plt.scatter()` for the plot, then add the title and axis labels.

plt.title('Study Hours vs Quiz Score')
plt.xlabel('Study Hours')
plt.ylabel('Quiz Score')

markdown:

- Set the y-axis label to `Revenue ($)`.
- Make the bars purple.
- Display the chart.

Try `plt.bar(departments, revenue, color='purple')`, then `plt.title('Department Revenue')` and `plt.ylabel('Revenue ($)')`.
solution_code:
plt.bar(departments, revenue, color='purple')
plt.title('Department Revenue')
plt.ylabel('Revenue ($)')

title: Sprint Output with Grid
markdown:
### The Scenario
A project manager wants a clearer chart showing tasks completed across development sprints.

### The Task
- Set the figure size to `(8, 4)`.
- Use `plt.plot()` to chart `sprints` vs `tasks_completed`.
- Turn the grid on.
- Set the title to `Sprint Output`.
- Display the chart.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sprints = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
tasks_completed = [12, 18, 17, 22, 24]

# Create your chart below



plt.show()
validation_code:
fig = plt.gcf()
ax = plt.gca()
width, height = fig.get_size_inches()
assert abs(width - 8) < 0.1 and abs(height - 4) < 0.1, 'Set the figure size to 8 by 4.'
assert len(ax.lines) == 1, 'We expected exactly one line on the chart.'
assert any(line.get_visible() for line in ax.get_xgridlines() + ax.get_ygridlines()), 'Turn the grid on using plt.grid(True).'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Sprint Output', 'Set the title to exactly "Sprint Output".'
hints: First create a figure with the requested size, then draw the line and enable the grid.
Use `plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))`, `plt.plot()`, and `plt.grid(True)`.
Try `plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))`, then `plt.plot(sprints, tasks_completed)`, `plt.grid(True)`, and `plt.title('Sprint Output')`.
solution_code:
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
plt.plot(sprints, tasks_completed)
plt.grid(True)
plt.title('Sprint Output')

title: Project Completion Range
markdown:
### The Scenario
A team lead wants a completion chart that always shows the full 0 to 100 percent scale.

### The Task
- Use `plt.plot()` to chart `weeks` vs `completion`.
- Set the y-axis limits from `0` to `100`.
- Set the title to `Project Completion`.
- Set the y-axis label to `Completion (%)`.
- Display the chart.
starting_code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

weeks = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
completion = [10, 22, 38, 55, 74, 88]

# Create your chart below



plt.show()
validation_code:
ax = plt.gca()
assert len(ax.lines) == 1, 'We expected exactly one line on the chart.'
ymin, ymax = ax.get_ylim()
assert abs(ymin - 0) < 0.1 and abs(ymax - 100) < 0.1, 'Set the y-axis limits to 0 and 100.'
assert ax.get_title() == 'Project Completion', 'Set the title to exactly "Project Completion".'
assert ax.get_ylabel() == 'Completion (%)', 'Set the y-axis label to exactly "Completion (%)".'
hints: Plot the progress line, then force the y-axis to show the entire percentage scale.
Use `plt.plot()` and then `plt.ylim(0, 100)`.
Try `plt.plot(weeks, completion)`, then `plt.ylim(0, 100)`, `plt.title('Project Completion')`, and `plt.ylabel('Completion (%)')`.
solution_code:
plt.plot(weeks, completion)
plt.ylim(0, 100)
plt.title('Project Completion')
plt.ylabel('Completion (%)')

months = ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May']
